content: Instances where the Upper Limits (ULs) were exceeded are documented and reported in the results below. The Population Reference Intake (PRI) values are derived from the US/Canadian Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs) (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2019) and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) Dietary Reference Values (DRVs) (EFSA, 2017). The abbreviations used are as follows: AI = Adequate Intake; PRI = Population Reference Intake; RDA = Recommended Dietary Allowance; RI = Reference Intake range. For fat intake as a percentage of energy for children aged 1–3 years, 35% represents the lower end of the EFSA Reference Intake range. A single value was required for the target, and after consultation with the Guideline Development Group (GDG), the lower end of the range was selected. Nutrient content is expressed per liter of human milk. Table 5 provides the nutrient composition of breast milk, including both target nutrients and other reported nutrients. The footnotes in the table are adapted from the Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee (DGAC). Sensitivity analyses were added to the original plan, focusing on best-case scenarios where no iron gap was observed, despite low intake of animal-source protein foods. The nutrient values provided are specific to milk composition at more than six months postpartum. The nutrient amounts represent the mean concentrations published in reports used to develop the US/Canadian Dietary Reference Intakes for infants, with exceptions for energy, total fat, and iron. For energy, a value of 680 kcal/L was based on compiled evidence regarding the metabolizable energy of human milk (Reilly, Ashworth, and Wells, 2005). For total fat, the mean value from the DRI report for older infants (ages 6–12 months) of 38 g/L was used (Institute of Medicine, 2005a). The contribution of iron from human milk after six months of age was rounded down to zero. Human breast milk was included as an item in the Optifood model food list, along with its associated food composition data, and quantities were defined in grams. The selected Nutrient Reference Values (NRVs) were based on data for infants aged 2.9 months. Food groups and subgroups were utilized in various ways. Quantitative parameters were developed at both the food group and subgroup levels, specifying maximum weekly consumption values in grams. Based on nutrient profiles, the Optifood model selected specific amounts of various food subgroups and groups, up to the maximum allowable amounts, to meet target nutrient needs. Modeling was conducted at the food subgroup level rather than the item level due to the wide variability of individual food items across geographic settings. Food subgroups were chosen to reflect items commonly consumed by infants and young children (IYC) in most settings. Broad food groups used in the analysis included: 1. Starchy staple foods (grains, white roots, tubers, and plantains) 2. Fruits 3. Vegetables 4. Dairy 5. All other protein foods (meat, poultry, fish, eggs, nuts, seeds, legumes, soy foods) 6. Added fats and oils Excluding added fats and oils, the first five groups align with the most common food group sets in national dietary guidelines globally. Food subgroups were carefully selected to ensure meaningful differences in nutrient profiles and to be widely recognizable to nutritionists globally. National authorities are expected to adapt global guidance into population-level recommendations, facilitated by the sensible selection of food subgroups. The development of food subgroups considered various sources, including US and Australian food pattern modeling exercises, previous Optifood studies, and WHO/UNICEF infant and young child feeding (IYCF) dietary diversity indicators. Further division into subgroups was advised when consumption quantities (in grams per day) varied significantly among item types (e.g., bread vs. dry cereal grains). Preliminary nutrient profiles for subgroups were developed, and outliers or unusual nutrient patterns were examined. For example, liver was separated from other organ meats due to its distinct nutrient profile and higher consumption frequency. Global culinary uses were also considered. For instance, peppers and tomatoes were grouped together as they are common sauce ingredients in many cuisines and are rich in vitamins A and C, unlike onions, which were classified with other vegetables. Unhealthy food and beverage items consumed by infants and young children were grouped into categories such as: Sweet beverages (non-dairy) Sweet baked goods (cakes, cookies, donuts) Sugar confections (candies, jellies, chocolate) Salty and/or fried snack foods and fast foods (chips, crisps, fried savory snacks, instant noodles) These categories align with sentinel unhealthy items identified in WHO/UNICEF IYCF indicators. Nutrient profiles for these subgroups were not comprehensively developed; instead, representative items were selected for inclusion in later modeling stages. Fortified items included in the modeling, based on GDG input, were: Multiple micronutrient powders (MNP) Small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) Fortified complementary foods The global food item list aimed to reflect foods consumed by infants and young children across diverse geographic and cultural settings. Mixed dishes were excluded due to their variability, but their ingredients were included when disaggregated in data sources. Steps in developing the list included extracting food item lists from diverse sources, excluding rarely consumed items, categorizing items into food groups and subgroups, and matching each item to an appropriate entry in a food composition database. Less healthy items were matched to healthier alternatives (e.g., fried meats to stewed meats, processed cheese to unprocessed cheese). Initial models focused on unfortified diets to identify nutrient gaps, with fortified items added in later stages. The number of unique food items per subgroup was summarized, reflecting exclusions and clustering of similar items.
